title: Who Gets to Set the Size of the Court
hook: Nine justices feels constitutional. It is not — the number is ordinary law, which is exactly why proposals to freeze it at nine keep appearing.
key_points: The U.S. Constitution creates a Supreme Court but does not fix how many justices sit on it; the number is set by statute.
That makes court expansion, often called court-packing, achievable through ordinary legislation rather than constitutional amendment.
Freezing the number instead requires an amendment: two-thirds of both chambers, then ratification by the states.
Per SCOTUSblog, House Speaker Mike Johnson announced a September 2026 vote on a constitutional amendment capping the Court at nine justices.
Johnson said nine justices has been the model that served the country for many years, and framed the vote as a response to calls to expand the Court.
The two-thirds threshold means such amendments rarely pass, so the vote functions partly as a recorded position for every member.
content_html: Most people assume the Supreme Court has nine justices because the Constitution says so. It does not. The Constitution creates the Court and leaves its size to Congress, which is why the number has been a live political question at several points in American history.
extra_html: That statutory footing cuts both ways. Because the size is set by ordinary law, a determined majority could enlarge the Court without amending anything — the possibility usually called court-packing. And because it is ordinary law, any promise not to do so is also ordinary law, repealable by the next majority. Entrenching the number therefore means going to Article V. SCOTUSblog's Kelsey Dallas and Amy Howe report that House Speaker Mike Johnson announced a September 2026 House vote on a constitutional amendment capping the Court at nine, saying that "the nine justices of the Supreme Court has been the model that has served this country for many, many years," and framing the vote as a response to calls from the left to expand the Court. An amendment needs two-thirds of both chambers before it even reaches the states for ratification, a threshold almost nothing clears in a closely divided Congress — so the immediate effect of such a vote is to put every member on the record. Both features are worth carrying forward: the durability of a rule depends on what kind of law it is, and a doomed vote can still be a deliberate political act. (This card describes the U.S. federal judiciary specifically.)

related.title: Supreme Court Term Limits
related.hook: U.S. Supreme Court justices serve for life — unusual among democracies. A recurring reform would swap that for fixed terms. Why the idea keeps returning, and why it's so hard to enact.

related.title: The Judiciary & Judicial Review
related.hook: Courts don't just settle disputes between people — through judicial review, many can also strike down a law or an official act that violates the constitution.

related.title: Amending a Constitution
related.hook: A constitution has to last — but not freeze. Amendment rules let it change deliberately, usually demanding more agreement than an ordinary law.

related.hook: Separating power isn't enough — each branch also gets tools to limit the others, so power keeps power in check.

flashcards.prompt: What sets the number of justices on the U.S. Supreme Court?
flashcards.back_html: An ordinary statute. The Constitution establishes the Court but leaves its size to Congress — which is why changing the number needs only legislation, while locking it in needs an amendment.

flashcards.prompt: Why does capping the Court at nine require a constitutional amendment rather than a law?

choices.text: A statute can be repealed by a later Congress, so only an amendment makes the cap durable
The Supreme Court must approve any statute about its own size
Federal courts are governed exclusively by state constitutions

flashcards.explanation_html: A future majority could simply change a statutory cap. Entrenchment is the whole point of routing it through Article V.

flashcards.prompt: What does the two-thirds threshold imply about the political function of such a vote?

choices.text: Passage is unlikely, so the vote mainly puts every member on the record
It guarantees the amendment takes effect immediately
It lets the House amend the Constitution without the Senate or states

flashcards.explanation_html: SCOTUSblog reports the speaker framing the vote as forcing a public position — a common use of amendment votes that cannot clear the bar.
